analysis.one_liner: Stops states from taking deceased Medicaid patients' homes to repay care costs.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 21 House Democrats, never received a hearing or a vote: it sat in a House subcommittee until Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, states must try to recover Medicaid spending from the estate of a person who received long-term care, which can mean placing a lien on or taking the family home after the person dies. This bill would repeal that federal requirement, bar states from collecting the cost of Medicaid benefits from estates going forward, and require states to withdraw existing property liens within 90 days. It would keep homes in families instead of handing them over to repay the state.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs and surviving family members of people who received Medicaid long-term care, especially older adults who own a home. Today, a widow or widower's heirs can lose the house to estate recovery after the state pays for nursing home or home care; this bill would end that, requiring states to drop existing liens within 90 days [S2, S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families of Medicaid long-term care recipients

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the federal requirement that states run a Medicaid Estate Recovery Program, so states could no longer pursue repayment of medical benefits from a deceased person's estate [S2, S3].
Bars states from initiating, maintaining, or collecting recovery for Medicaid benefits correctly paid, and requires states to withdraw any existing property liens within 90 days of enactment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: State Medicaid programs, and ultimately taxpayers generally, lose the money recovered from estates, which helps offset the cost of long-term care for Medicaid recipients [S2, S3].

drawbacks.text: Estate recovery returns real money to Medicaid. Ending it removes that revenue, shifting the cost of long-term care from the estates of people who used the program onto state budgets and taxpayers [S2, S3].

The bill applies broadly to 'any medical assistance correctly paid,' not just long-term care, so a good-faith objection is that a person who received an unusual, expensive Medicaid benefit could pass a large unpaid bill to the public instead of their estate [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and personal: fewer families lose a home after a parent's death. The cost is real but diffuse: states and taxpayers absorb the recovered dollars. A narrower bill limited to long-term-care recovery (with current-law exceptions for surviving spouses already in place) would have cost less; this version sweeps in all Medicaid benefits.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its Health subcommittee, and died there without a hearing or a vote when the Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on February 9, 2022 with 20 Democratic cosponsors, all referrals landing in the House Energy and Commerce Committee [S1, S4, S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, where no further action was taken before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State Medicaid programs kept their estate recovery revenue and the existing rules stayed in place; families facing liens got no relief.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State Medicaid programs kept recovering estates

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and brought the first 20 cosponsors on board.

against.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a committee vote; it sat in the Health subcommittee for the rest of the Congress and died there.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no committee or floor vote was ever recorded on the bill [S1, S4, S5].

industries.note: States currently recoup the cost of long-term care from recipients' estates, including homes; the bill would end that revenue stream and require dropping existing liens [S2, S3]. The program's financial interest in collecting from estates runs against families' interest in keeping the house.
Estate recovery returns federal and state dollars that offset Medicaid spending; without it, the cost of long-term care shifts to general taxpayers [S2, S3].
